claim: Infertility affects approximately one in six couples worldwide.
source: Infertility is a global public health and social problem that affects approximately one in six couples worldwide (Cox et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2022.

claim: Male infertility accounts for half of infertile cases.
source: Male infertility, which accounts for half of infertile cases, is a multifactorial disease with common phenotypes, including oligo/azoospermia (poor sperm count or absence of spermatozoa); teratozoospermia (aberrant sperm morphology); asthenozoospermia (weakened sperm motility); and a combination of these phenotypes, such as asthenoteratozoospermia, oligoasthenozoospermia, oligoteratozoospermia, and oligoasthenoteratozoospermia (Eisenberg et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eisenberg et al., 2023 and Agarwal et al., 2015.

claim: More than 40 genes have been identified as pathogenic genes of MMAF.
source: To date, more than 40 genes have been identified as pathogenic genes of MMAF, but these genes can only explain approximately 60% of MMAF-affected cases (Wang et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021; Houston et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021; Houston et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2021.

claim: Identified MMAF genes can only explain approximately 60% of MMAF-affected cases.
source: To date, more than 40 genes have been identified as pathogenic genes of MMAF, but these genes can only explain approximately 60% of MMAF-affected cases (Wang et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021; Houston et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2021; Houston et al., 2021; Jiao et al., 2021.

claim: The sperm flagella contains a '9+2' microtubular arrangement consisting of nine microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair of singlet microtubules.
source: The motility of a sperm is driven by its rhythmically beating flagella, and at the center of the flagella lies a conserved axonemal structure, containing the '9+2' microtubular arrangement: a ring of nine microtubule doublets (MTDs) surrounding a central pair (CP) of singlet microtubules.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about sperm flagellar structure.

claim: The ODA and IDA are ATPase-based protein complexes that drive sperm motility.
source: The ODA and IDA are ATPase-based protein complexes that drive the movement between the A tubule and the neighboring B tubule of the next doublet, producing the original force for sperm motility (Burgess et al., 2003; Linck et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 2003 and Linck et al., 2016.

claim: DNAH3 is highly expressed in testes of humans and mice.
source: DNAH3 is an evolutionarily conserved IDA-associated protein and is highly expressed in testes of humans and mice (Chapelin et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chapelin et al., 1997.

claim: Deficient DNAH3 impairs sperm motility in Drosophila and cattle.
source: Deficient DNAH3 has been shown to impair sperm motility in Drosophila and cattle (Karak et al., 2015; Modiba et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karak et al., 2015 and Modiba et al., 2022.

claim: DNAH3 has been identified as a novel breast cancer candidate gene.
source: In humans, DNAH3 has been identified as a novel breast cancer candidate gene (Hamdi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hamdi et al., 2018.

claim: Four biallelic variations in DNAH3 were identified in four unrelated Han Chinese patients with asthenoteratozoospermia using whole-exome sequencing.
source: In the present study, we identified four biallelic variations in DNAH3 in four unrelated Han Chinese patients with asthenoteratozoospermia using whole-exome sequencing (WES).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from whole-exome sequencing performed in the study.

claim: Patient 1 has a compound heterozygous mutation of c.3590C>T (p.Pro1197Leu) and c.3590C>G (p.Pro1197Arg) in DNAH3.
source: a compound heterozygous mutation of c.3590C>T (p.Pro1197Leu) and c.3590C>G (p.Pro1197Arg) in Patient 1
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and Sanger sequencing confirmation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Patient 2 has a homozygous missense mutation of c.4837G>T (p.Ala1613Ser) in DNAH3.
source: a homozygous missense mutation of c.4837G>T (p.Ala1613Ser) in Patient 2
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and Sanger sequencing confirmation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Patient 3 has a compound heterozygous mutation of c.5587del (p.Leu1863*) and c.10355C>T (p.Ser3452Leu) in DNAH3.
source: a compound heterozygous mutation of c.5587del (p.Leu1863*) and c.10355C>T (p.Ser3452Leu) in Patient 3
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and Sanger sequencing confirmation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Patient 4 has a compound heterozygous mutation of c.2314C>T (p.Arg772Trp) and c.4045G>A (p.Asp1349Asn) in DNAH3.
source: a compound heterozygous mutation of c.2314C>T (p.Arg772Trp) and c.4045G>A (p.Asp1349Asn) in Patient 4
evidence: The claim is supported by WES data and Sanger sequencing confirmation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: All patients showed extremely reduced sperm motility and a high proportion of sperm tail defects.
source: Importantly, routine semen analysis revealed that all patients showed extremely reduced sperm motility and a high proportion of sperm tail defects (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by semen analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: The identified DNAH3 variants were predicted to be potentially deleterious by SIFT, PolyPhen-2, MutationTaster, and CADD.
source: These variants either were not recorded or had an extremely low frequency in East Asian population in multiple public population databases, including the ExAC browser, GnomAD and the 1000 Genomes Project, and were predicted to be potentially deleterious by SIFT (https://sift.bii.a-star.edu.sg/), PolyPhen-2 (http://genetics.bwh.harvard.edu/pph2/), MutationTaster (https://www.mutationtaster.org/), and CADD (https://cadd.gs.washington.edu/; Table 2; Ng and Henikoff, 2003; Adzhubei et al., 2010; Schwarz et al., 2014; Rentzsch et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational predictions using established bioinformatics tools and citations to the methods (Ng and Henikoff, 2003; Adzhubei et al., 2010; Schwarz et al., 2014; Rentzsch et al., 2019).

claim: The variant sites in DNAH3 are highly conserved across species.
source: Moreover, the variant sites are localized in several domains of the DNAH3 protein and are highly conserved across species (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by conservation analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DNAH3 was exclusively resided in the tail and concentrated in the midpiece of control sperm.
source: Strikingly, immunofluorescence staining revealed that DNAH3 was exclusively resided in the tail and concentrated in the midpiece of control sperm.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The fluorescence signal of DNAH3 was hardly detected in the patients' spermatozoa.
source: However, the fluorescence signal of DNAH3 was hardly detected in the patients' spermatozoa (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Western blotting analysis indicated that DNAH3 variants led to disrupted expression of DNAH3.
source: Additionally, subsequent western blotting analysis yielded consistent results with immunofluorescence staining, indicating that these variants led to disrupted expression of DNAH3 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The tails of sperm from the patients exhibited a typical MMAF phenotype, including coiled, short, bent, irregular, and/or absent flagella.
source: Notably, the tails of sperm from the patients exhibited a typical phenotype associated with MMAF, including coiled, short, bent, irregular, and/or absent flagella (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Papanicolaou staining and SEM analysis shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spermatozoa from the patients showed absent or disordered CPs, MTDs, and ODFs in different regions of the flagella.
source: Compared to the integrated and well-organized '9 + 2' axonemal arrangement of the sperm flagella from the normal control, spermatozoa from the patients showed absent or disordered CPs, MTDs, and outer dense fibers (ODFs) in different regions of the flagella (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IDAs of sperm flagella of the patients were hardly captured compared to the control.
source: Interestingly, the IDAs of sperm flagella of the patients were hardly captured compared to the control (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Dissolved mitochondrial material was observed in the midpiece of sperm flagella of the patients.
source: Additionally, in the midpiece of sperm flagella of the patients, dissolved mitochondrial material was also observed evidently under TEM (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: TOM20 signals in the sperm from the patients were considerably diminished, indicating disrupted mitochondrial function.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to the robust TOM20 signals observed in the normal control, the TOM20 signals in the sperm from the patients were considerably diminished, indicating a disrupted mitochondrial function (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of TOM20 shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dnah3 was predominantly expressed in the mouse testis.
source: qPCR results revealed that Dnah3 was predominantly expressed in the mouse testis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dnah3 expression was significantly elevated beginning on postnatal Day 22, peaked at postnatal Day 30, and maintained a stable expression level thereafter.
source: Moreover, when observing the expression of Dnah3 in testes from mice at different postnatal days, we found that Dnah3 expression was significantly elevated beginning on postnatal Day 22, peaked at postnatal Day 30, and maintained a stable expression level thereafter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: DNAH3 was expressed in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes and spermatogonia and then obviously in the flagellum of early and late spermatids.
source: In addition, germ cells at different stages were isolated from the testes of humans and mice and were stained with anti-DNAH3 antibody. The results showed that DNAH3 was expressed in the cytoplasm of spermatocytes and spermatogonia and then obviously in the flagellum of early and late spermatids (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Dnah3 KO mice were generated using CRISPR‒Cas9 technology.
source: Considering the absent expression of DNAH3 in the patient sperm, we generated Dnah3 KO mice using CRISPR‒Cas9 technology to further confirm the essential role of DNAH3 in spermatogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental method and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Dnah3 was null in KO mice as confirmed by PCR, qPCR, and immunofluorescence staining.
source: PCR, qPCR, and immunofluorescence staining were used to confirm that Dnah3 was null in KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR, qPCR, and immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B–E.

claim: There were no histological differences in the lung, brain, eye, or oviduct between wild-type and Dnah3 KO mice.
source: H&E staining further revealed that there were no histological differences in the lung, brain, eye, or oviduct between wild-type (WT) and Dnah3 KO mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claim: No obvious abnormalities in ciliary development were observed in the lung, brain, eye, or oviduct in Dnah3 KO mice compared to WT mice.
source: In addition, no obvious abnormalities in ciliary development were observed in these organs in KO mice compared to WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Dnah3 KO female mice were fertile with normal oocyte development.
source: The Dnah3 KO female mice were fertile with normal oocyte development (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining of ovary tissue shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: Dnah3 KO male mice were completely infertile.
source: However, the Dnah3 KO male mice were completely infertile (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no detectable difference in the testis/body weight ratio of Dnah3 KO mice when compared to WT mice.
source: There was no detectable difference in the testis/body weight ratio of Dnah3 KO mice when compared to WT mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by testis/body weight ratio data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Sperm isolated from the cauda epididymis of Dnah3 KO mice were slightly decreased, and nearly all sperm were completely immobile.
source: Moreover, subsequent computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) also showed that sperm isolated from the cauda epididymis were slightly decreased, and nearly all sperm were completely immobile (Table 3, Figure 4—video 1 and Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by CASA data presented in Table 3.

claim: Morphological defects in partial spermatozoa from Dnah3 KO mice include coiled, bent, and irregular flagella, as well as aberrant heads and acephalic spermatozoa.
source: Papanicolaou staining and SEM analysis revealed morphological defects in partial spermatozoa from Dnah3 KO mice, including coiled, bent, and irregular flagella, as well as aberrant heads and acephalic spermatozoa (Figure 4—figure supplement 6A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Papanicolaou staining and SEM analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A and 6B.

claim: The sperm flagella of Dnah3 KO mice exhibited an absence of almost all the IDAs.
source: However, in contrast to the clear display of an IDA and an ODA on the A-tube of each microtubule doublet in the sperm flagella of WT mice, the sperm flagella of Dnah3 KO mice exhibited an absence of almost all the IDAs (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 6D.

claim: Disrupted mitochondria of spermatozoa from Dnah3 KO mice were observed, manifested by dilated intermembrane spaces and dissolved mitochondrial material.
source: In addition, the disrupted mitochondria of spermatozoa from Dnah3 KO mice were also observed under TEM, as manifested by the dilated intermembrane spaces and dissolved mitochondrial material (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM analysis shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 6E.

claim: SLC25A4 signals in Dnah3 KO sperm were significantly diminished compared to WT sperm, indicating impaired mitochondrial function.
source: Strikingly, compared to the bright fluorescence signals in the midpiece of WT sperm, the signals Dnah3 KO were significantly diminished (Figure 4D), indicating impaired mitochondrial function.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of SLC25A4 shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DNAH1, DNAH6, and DNALI1 were almost invisible along the sperm flagella of the patients when compared to control.
source: The immunofluorescence data showed that DNAH1/DNAH6 and DNALI1, corresponding to the heavy and light intermediate chains of the IDAs (Walton et al., 2023), respectively, were almost invisible along the sperm flagella of the patients when compared to control (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 5A–C and citation to Walton et al., 2023.

claim: Western blotting analysis of sperm lysates from the patients showed decreased expression of DNAH1, DNAH6, and DNALI1.
source: Consistent results were obtained in our subsequent western blotting analysis of sperm lysates from the patients (Figure 5D–F), indicating that DNAH3 may manipulate the assembly of IDA through regulating the expression of IDA-associated proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: DNAH8, DNAH17, and DNAI1 were readily detectable in the patients' sperm flagella and were comparable to the control.
source: In contrast, DNAH8/DNAH17 and DNAI1, corresponding to the heavy and intermediate chains of ODAs (Whitfield et al., 2019), were readily detectable in the patients' sperm flagella and were comparable to the control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that DNAH3 may not regulate the expression of ODA-associated proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C and citation to Whitfield et al., 2019.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining and western blotting analysis of DNAH1, DNAH6, DNALI1, DNAH8, DNAH17 and DNAI1 on sperm from Dnah3 KO mice yielded results consistent with those of the patients.
source: We also performed immunofluorescence staining and western blotting analysis of DNAH1, DNAH6, DNALI1, DNAH8, DNAH17 and DNAI1 on sperm from Dnah3 KO mice, and the results observed were consistent with those of the patients (Figure 6A–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and western blotting data shown in Figure 6A–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The wife of Patient 1 underwent one ICSI attempt with a fertilization rate of 80.95% (17/21).
source: The wife of Patient 1 underwent one ICSI attempt. A total of 21 metaphase II (MII) oocytes were retrieved and microinjected, of which 17 oocytes were successfully fertilized (17/21, 80.95%) and cleaved (17/17, 100%).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI treatment data presented in Table 4.

claim: The wife of Patient 1 achieved clinical pregnancy, and the pregnancy is ongoing.
source: Two blastocysts were transferred, one of which was implanted. She eventually achieved clinical pregnancy, and the pregnancy is ongoing (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI treatment outcome data presented in Table 4.

claim: The partner of Patient 3 achieved clinical pregnancy, and the pregnancy is ongoing.
source: One blastocyst was transferred and implanted. She achieved clinical pregnancy, and the pregnancy is ongoing (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI treatment outcome data presented in Table 4.

claim: The wife of Patient 4 underwent four failed ICSI attempts.
source: The wife of Patient 4 underwent four failed ICSI attempts.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI treatment outcome data presented in Table 4.

claim: There was no difference in the fertilization rate or 2 cell and blastocyst embryo formation rates between the Dnah3 KO and WT groups in ICSI treatment.
source: There was no difference in the percentage of 2 cell and blastocyst-stage embryos between the KO and WT groups (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICSI outcome data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: ICSI might be a favorable treatment for male infertility caused by DNAH3 deficiency.
source: Collectively, we observed successful ICSI outcomes in two out of four DNAH3-deficient patients and Dnah3 KO male mice and therefore suggested ICSI as an optional treatment for infertile men harboring biallelic pathogenic variants in DNAH3, and the additional female risk factors for infertility should not be excluded in the failed patients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the ICSI treatment outcomes in patients and mice.

claim: DNAH3 is a novel pathogenic gene for asthenoteratozoospermia.
source: This study revealed DNAH3 as a novel pathogenic gene of asthenoteratozoospermia, and the findings provide valuable suggestions for the clinical diagnosis and treatment of male infertility.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined data from patients and Dnah3 KO mice showing that DNAH3 deficiency causes asthenoteratozoospermia.

claim: Meng et al. reported DNAH3 mutations in asthenoteratozoospermia affected patients, revealing multiple morphological defects in sperm tail.
source: Recently, Meng et al. reported DNAH3 mutations in asthenoteratozoospermia affected patients, revealing multiple morphological defects in sperm tail (Meng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2024.

claim: Ultrastructural abnormalities of the flagellar axoneme in patients with DNAH3 mutations were characterized by a disrupted '9+2' arrangement and the notable absence of IDAs.
source: Moreover, ultrastructural abnormalities of the flagellar axoneme in the patients were evident in these patients, characterized by a disrupted '9+2' arrangement and the notable absence of IDAs (Meng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2024.

claim: Meng et al. generated Dnah3 KO mice, which were infertile and exhibited moderate morphological abnormalities.
source: Additionally, they generated Dnah3 KO mice, which were infertile and exhibited moderate morphological abnormalities (Meng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2024.

claim: In Meng et al.'s study, the '9+2' microtubule arrangement in the flagella of their Dnah3 KO mice remained intact, but the IDAs on the microtubules were partially absent.
source: While the '9+2' microtubule arrangement in the flagella of their Dnah3 KO mice remained intact, the IDAs on the microtubules were partially absent (Meng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2024.

claim: DNAH3 may play crucial yet distinct roles in human and mouse male reproduction.
source: Both studies suggest that DNAH3 may play crucial yet distinct roles in human and mouse male reproduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparing the phenotypes observed in humans and mice in both studies.

claim: Male infertility caused by DNAH3 mutations follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
source: We revealed that male infertility caused by DNAH3 mutations follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, as confirmed through Sanger sequencing of the patients' families.
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data from the patients' families shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DNAH3 was initially expressed in the cytoplasm of spermatogonia and spermatocytes, and then it clearly transferred into the flagellum of early and late spermatids.
source: Initially, DNAH3 was expressed in the cytoplasm of spermatogonia and spermatocytes, and then it clearly transferred into the flagellum of early and late spermatids.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: DNAH3 deficiency had no impact on ciliary development in the oviduct or on oogenesis in mice, resulting in normal female fertility.
source: We further found that DNAH3 deficiency had no impact on ciliary development in the oviduct or on oogenesis in mice, resulting in normal female fertility.
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining and immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: In the absence of DNAH3 in both humans and mice, the expression of IDA-associated proteins, including DNAH1, DNAH6, and DNALI1, was decreased, while the expression of ODA-associated proteins remained unaffected.
source: Moreover, in the absence of DNAH3 in both humans and mice, the expression of IDA-associated proteins, including DNAH1, DNAH6, and DNALI1, was decreased, while the expression of ODA-associated proteins remained unaffected, indicating that DNAH3 is involved in sperm axonemal development, specifically through its role in the assembly of IDAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and western blotting data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) affects at least one in 7554 individuals.
source: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD, MIM: 244400) is a genetic disorder affecting at least one in 7554 individuals (Hannah et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hannah et al., 2022.

claim: Male infertility associated with sperm defects is highly prevalent (up to 75%) among individuals with PCD.
source: It has been suggested that male infertility associated with sperm defects is highly prevalent (up to 75%) among individuals with PCD (Vanaken et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vanaken et al., 2017.

claim: Axonemal defects caused by variants within DNAH5, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH9 and DNAH11 are causative factors for PCD.
source: Axonemal defects caused by variants within DNAH family members, including DNAH5, DNAH6, DNAH7, DNAH9 and DNAH11, are causative factors for PCD (Hornef et al., 2006; Guan et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hornef et al., 2006; Guan et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022.

claim: Deficiency in PCD-causing DNAHs has been associated with male infertility.
source: Moreover, deficiency in these PCD-causing DNAHs has also been associated with male infertility (Jiao et al., 2021; Sironen et al., 2020; Tu et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022; Fliegauf et al., 2005; Fassad et al., 2018; Zuccarello et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jiao et al., 2021; Sironen et al., 2020; Tu et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2022; Fliegauf et al., 2005; Fassad et al., 2018; Zuccarello et al., 2008.

claim: DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH8, DNAH10, DNAH12, and DNAH17 are suggested to be pathogenic genes of isolated male infertility.
source: Additionally, other DNAHs, such as DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH8, DNAH10, DNAH12, and DNAH17, are suggested to be pathogenic genes of isolated male infertility (Ben Khelifa et al., 2014; Hwang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Whitfield et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ben Khelifa et al., 2014; Hwang et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021; Whitfield et al., 2019.

claim: None of the patients with DNAH3 deficiency reported experiencing any of the principal symptoms associated with PCD.
source: Intriguingly, in our study, none of the patients with DNAH3 deficiency reported experiencing any of the principal symptoms associated with PCD.
evidence: The claim is based on clinical observation of the patients in the study.

claim: Dnah3 KO mice exhibited normal ciliary development in the lung, brain, eye, and oviduct.
source: Additionally, our Dnah3 KO mice exhibited normal ciliary development in the lung, brain, eye, and oviduct.
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining and immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: DNAH3 may play a more important role in sperm flagellar development than in other motile cilia functions.
source: These combined observations suggest that DNAH3 may play a more important role in sperm flagellar development than in other motile cilia functions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that DNAH3 deficiency causes male infertility but not PCD symptoms.

claim: Infertile males with variants in DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH7, and DNAH8 have a favorable prognosis with ICSI.
source: It has been demonstrated that infertile males with variants in DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH7, and DNAH8 have a favorable prognosis (Liu et al., 2020; Long et al., 2023; Wambergue et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2020; Long et al., 2023; Wambergue et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2021; Wei et al., 2021.

claim: Patients with variants in DNAH17 have poor outcomes after ICSI treatment.
source: while patients with variants in DNAH17 have poor outcomes after ICSI treatment (Whitfield et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whitfield et al., 2019 and Zheng et al., 2021.

claim: The ICSI outcomes in male infertility caused by DNAH6 variants may depend on the specific mutation or be controversial.
source: Meanwhile, the ICSI outcomes in male infertility caused by DNAH6 variants may depend on the specific mutation or be controversial (Tu et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tu et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2018.

claim: All variants in DNAH3 observed in the four patients led to a complete absence of DNAH3 expression.
source: Remarkably, despite the diverse variants within DNAH3 observed in the four patients, all variants led to a complete absence of DNAH3 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining and western blotting data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: In the study from Meng et al., one patient carrying DNAH3 variants received ICSI treatment, and the partner obtained clinical pregnancy.
source: Importantly, in the study from Meng et al., one patient carrying DNAH3 variants received ICSI treatment, and the partner obtained clinical pregnancy (Meng et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng et al., 2024.

claim: DNAH3 is an evolutionarily conserved IDA-associated protein.
source: DNAH3 is an evolutionarily conserved IDA-associated protein and is highly expressed in testes of humans and mice (Chapelin et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chapelin et al., 1997.

claim: DNAH3 is fundamental for male fertility.
source: Combined with similar findings in Dnah3 KO mice, we demonstrated that DNAH3 is fundamental for male fertility.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined data from patients and Dnah3 KO mice showing that DNAH3 deficiency causes male infertility.

claim: DNAH3 may manipulate the assembly of IDA through regulating the expression of IDA-associated proteins.
source: Consistent results were obtained in our subsequent western blotting analysis of sperm lysates from the patients (Figure 5D–F), indicating that DNAH3 may manipulate the assembly of IDA through regulating the expression of IDA-associated proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that DNAH3 deficiency leads to decreased expression of IDA-associated proteins.

claim: DNAH3 may not regulate the expression of ODA-associated proteins.
source: In contrast, DNAH8/DNAH17 and DNAI1, corresponding to the heavy and intermediate chains of ODAs (Whitfield et al., 2019), were readily detectable in the patients' sperm flagella and were comparable to the control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that DNAH3 may not regulate the expression of ODA-associated proteins.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that ODA-associated proteins remain unaffected in DNAH3-deficient sperm.

claim: Other IDA-associated proteins might be downstream effectors of DNAH3.
source: These findings suggested that other IDA-associated proteins might be downstream effectors of DNAH3, which needs more future research.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation from the observed decrease in IDA-associated proteins in DNAH3-deficient sperm.

claim: The different ICSI outcomes in patients with DNAH3 variants might be attributed to additional unexplained factors from the female partners.
source: Remarkably, despite the diverse variants within DNAH3 observed in the four patients, all variants led to a complete absence of DNAH3 expression. Additionally, we did not identify any pathogenic variants that associated with fertilization failure and early embryonic development in the two patients with failed ICSI outcomes. Therefore, these different ICSI outcomes might be attributed to additional unexplained factors from the female partners.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that all DNAH3 variants led to complete absence of DNAH3 expression, yet ICSI outcomes varied.

claim: Additional female risk factors for infertility should not be excluded in the failed ICSI patients.
source: Collectively, we observed successful ICSI outcomes in two out of four DNAH3-deficient patients and Dnah3 KO male mice and therefore suggested ICSI as an optional treatment for infertile men harboring biallelic pathogenic variants in DNAH3, and the additional female risk factors for infertility should not be excluded in the failed patients.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the varied ICSI outcomes in patients with DNAH3 variants.
